questions: Where is your hometown?
What do you like most about your hometown?
Has your hometown changed much since you were a child?

vocab.meaning: very close to
vocab.example: My university is just a stone's throw from where I grew up.

vocab.meaning: a large, spread-out residential area
vocab.example: It's turned into a sprawling suburb over the last decade.

vocab.meaning: a tightly connected group of people who know each other well
vocab.example: What I love most is the close-knit community — everyone still knows everyone.

vocab.meaning: a place seen as dull or unimportant
vocab.example: Growing up it felt like a quiet backwater, to be honest.

vocab.meaning: changed a great deal
vocab.example: The town centre has undergone significant changes since I was a kid.

vocab.meaning: to have spent one's whole early life in a place
vocab.example: I was born and raised there, so it's home in every sense.

vocab.meaning: beautiful natural views
vocab.example: It's known for its picturesque scenery, especially along the river.

vocab.meaning: very different from
vocab.example: The place now is a far cry from how I remember it as a kid.

models.text: So I'm actually from a fairly small city, and I still live there now, honestly. I'd say what I like most about it is that it's a really close-knit community — everyone kind of knows everyone, which sounds a bit much but it's actually really nice, especially compared to bigger cities where you barely know your neighbours.

I'm originally from a small town on the outskirts of the capital, though I don't live there anymore. Um, it's changed a lot, actually — when I go back now it's honestly a far cry from how I remember it as a kid, way more built up, so it barely feels like home sometimes.

bandTip: 🎯 Lexical Resource: notice Model B doesn't just say "it changed" — it says "undergone significant changes" and "a far cry from." Precise collocations like these, used naturally rather than forced in, are what separate Band 6-7 vocabulary from Band 8+.

questions: Do you work or are you a student?
What do you like about your job or course?
Is there anything you'd change about it?

vocab.meaning: something difficult to learn quickly
vocab.example: The first few months were a steep learning curve, to put it mildly.

vocab.meaning: practical, direct experience
vocab.example: What I value most is the hands-on experience — it's not just theory.

vocab.meaning: manage several tasks due at the same time
vocab.example: During exam season I'm constantly juggling multiple deadlines.

vocab.meaning: a standard office job
vocab.example: I never really pictured myself in a nine-to-five, but here I am.

vocab.meaning: become exhausted from overwork
vocab.example: If I'm honest, I did burn out a bit in my final year.

vocab.meaning: advance professionally
vocab.example: I'm not in a huge rush to climb the career ladder just yet.

vocab.meaning: the balance between job and personal life
vocab.example: The work-life balance here is genuinely better than my last job.

vocab.meaning: repetitive and boring
vocab.example: Some of the admin side can get pretty monotonous, not gonna lie.

models.text: I'm currently a student, actually, studying business at university. I'd say what I enjoy most is the hands-on experience we get through group projects — it's not just sitting in lectures, we actually apply things, which makes it feel a lot less monotonous than I expected.

I work full-time, in marketing. Honestly, the thing I like is the creative side of it, coming up with campaigns and so on — but if I'm being truthful, juggling multiple deadlines does mean the work-life balance isn't always great, so that's the one thing I'd probably change.

bandTip: 🎯 Fluency & Coherence: "if I'm being truthful" and "if I'm honest" are hedging phrases that let you soften an opinion naturally mid-answer — examiners read this as confident, native-like discourse management, not hesitation.

questions: How much time do you spend online every day?
What do you mainly use the internet for?
Do you think you rely on technology too much?

vocab.meaning: using a phone constantly
vocab.example: If I'm honest, I'm pretty much glued to my phone most evenings.

vocab.meaning: make routine tasks quicker and easier
vocab.example: Apps like that really streamline everyday tasks, like banking or shopping.

vocab.meaning: endlessly scrolling through negative news or content
vocab.example: I've had to actively stop myself doomscrolling before bed.

vocab.meaning: a period of avoiding screens/technology
vocab.example: I tried a digital detox last summer — lasted about two days.

vocab.meaning: very dependent on
vocab.example: I'd say I'm heavily reliant on my phone for pretty much everything now.

vocab.term: at the touch of a button
vocab.meaning: instantly and easily accessible
vocab.example: You can get almost any information at the touch of a button these days.

vocab.meaning: time spent using digital devices
vocab.example: My screen time report last week was honestly a bit alarming.

vocab.meaning: to disconnect from devices/technology
vocab.example: I try to unplug completely on Sundays, though it doesn't always work.

models.text: Probably too much, if I'm honest — I checked my screen time recently and it was well over five hours. Mostly it's for work messages and social media, though. I do think I'm heavily reliant on it, actually, to the point where I've started trying to unplug at least one evening a week.

I'd say a few hours, mainly for practical stuff — banking, maps, that sort of thing. It streamlines everyday tasks so much that I don't really see it as a bad habit, as long as you're not doomscrolling for hours, which I try to avoid.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "to the point where I've started trying to unplug" is a result clause — a Band 8+ grammar feature. Practice linking an idea to its consequence with "to the point where" instead of just saying "so."

questions: What do you usually do in your free time?
Have your hobbies changed since you were younger?
Do you prefer hobbies you do alone or with others?

vocab.meaning: relax after a period of work or stress
vocab.example: Reading is how I unwind after a long day.

vocab.meaning: start a new hobby or skill
vocab.example: I picked up photography during the pandemic, actually.

vocab.meaning: be abandoned or neglected over time
vocab.example: Piano lessons kind of fell by the wayside once I started university.

vocab.meaning: a way to express creativity
vocab.example: Painting's my creative outlet — I don't do it for anyone but myself.

vocab.meaning: rest and restore energy
vocab.example: Weekends are really about recharging my batteries.

vocab.meaning: something you learn to enjoy over time
vocab.example: Running was honestly an acquired taste for me.

vocab.meaning: an activity done alone
vocab.example: I actually enjoy solitary activities more than team ones.

vocab.meaning: become comfortable or established in something
vocab.example: It took a while to get into the swing of it, but I love it now.

models.text: It's changed a fair bit, actually — as a kid it was mostly sport, but these days I'd say reading and cooking are my main hobbies. I think a lot of the sportier stuff just fell by the wayside once I got busier with work, but cooking's become a proper creative outlet for me.

I'm someone who really needs other people involved, if I'm honest — solitary activities like reading never quite stuck for me. I play in a five-a-side football team every week, and it's less about the sport, really, more just a chance to unwind with friends.

bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: notice both models open with a clear stance ("it's changed a fair bit" / "I really need other people involved") before explaining — always answer the question directly first, then justify. Examiners mark down answers that bury the actual answer in the middle.

questions: Do you enjoy cooking?
What's your favourite type of food?
Do you think eating habits in your country are changing?

vocab.meaning: someone willing to try unusual foods
vocab.example: I'd call myself a fairly adventurous eater, to be honest.

vocab.meaning: food that provides emotional comfort, often simple
vocab.example: On a bad day, it's straight to comfort food for me.

vocab.meaning: made using raw ingredients, not pre-made
vocab.example: I try to cook from scratch as much as I can.

vocab.meaning: pre-prepared food requiring little effort
vocab.example: People are relying more on convenience food than they used to.

vocab.meaning: developed a liking for something over time
vocab.example: I've genuinely acquired a taste for spicy food since moving abroad.

vocab.meaning: not healthy at all
vocab.example: It's delicious, but it's a far cry from healthy, let's be honest.

vocab.meaning: while busy or moving around
vocab.example: A lot of people just eat on the go now, which wasn't the norm before.

vocab.meaning: a meal prepared at home, not bought
vocab.example: Nothing beats a proper home-cooked meal, honestly.

models.text: I do, yeah, quite a lot actually — I find it really relaxing, oddly enough. I try to cook from scratch most nights rather than relying on convenience food. My favourite is probably traditional food from my region, it's just proper comfort food for me.

models.angle: Not a cook, notices changing habits
models.text: Not really, if I'm honest, I'm not the best cook. I'd say eating habits are definitely changing where I'm from, though — people eat on the go a lot more now, which is a far cry from how my grandparents used to eat, always sitting down together.

bandTip: 🎯 Pronunciation: in Model B, stress "definitely" and "a lot more" — Part 1 examiners listen for natural sentence stress on the words carrying the opinion, not flat, even-weighted delivery.

questions: Do you have a big family?
Who are you closest to in your family?
How often do you see your extended family?

vocab.meaning: parents, siblings, and children
vocab.example: My immediate family is fairly small, just the four of us.

vocab.meaning: relatives beyond parents/siblings, e.g. cousins
vocab.example: My extended family, on the other hand, is huge.

vocab.meaning: family members are emotionally close
vocab.example: We're a close family, we speak most days actually.

vocab.meaning: gradually become less close
vocab.example: We did drift apart a bit once everyone moved to different cities.

vocab.meaning: a family member seen as different from the rest
vocab.example: I'm kind of the black sheep, I'm the only one who moved abroad.

vocab.meaning: admire and respect someone
vocab.example: I've always looked up to my older sister, if I'm honest.

vocab.meaning: maintain regular contact
vocab.example: We make an effort to keep in touch even though we're all busy.

vocab.meaning: a very close, connected family
vocab.example: We're a pretty tight-knit family, we get together most weekends.

models.text: I'd say a medium-sized immediate family, and then a fairly huge extended family on my mum's side. I'm probably closest to my older sister — I've always looked up to her, honestly, and we still speak almost every day even though she doesn't live nearby anymore.

My immediate family's fairly close, but my extended family, not so much, if I'm being honest — we did drift apart a bit once people started moving away for work. We try to keep in touch, but realistically I only see them once or twice a year now, maybe at a wedding or something.

bandTip: 🎯 Lexical Resource: "immediate family" vs "extended family" is a precise distinction many candidates miss, saying just "family" for both. Using the correct term for each shows topic-specific vocabulary control.

questions: What's your favourite season?
Does the weather affect your mood?
What's the weather like where you live at the moment?

vocab.meaning: moderate, not extreme temperatures
vocab.example: We're lucky, we've got a fairly mild climate here.

vocab.meaning: extremely hot weather
vocab.example: Summers can get to scorching heat, honestly unbearable at times.

vocab.meaning: dress warmly
vocab.example: You really have to bundle up once winter kicks in.

vocab.meaning: feeling slightly unwell
vocab.example: I always feel a bit under the weather when it's grey for weeks.

vocab.meaning: the transition between seasons
vocab.example: I actually love the change of season, especially autumn coming in.

vocab.meaning: spoil or dampen an occasion or mood
vocab.example: Rain can really put a damper on weekend plans here.

vocab.meaning: informally, feeling low during darker months
vocab.example: I get a bit low in winter, almost seasonal-affective-disorder-ish, honestly.

vocab.meaning: cool, fresh air typical of autumn
vocab.example: There's nothing like that crisp autumn air first thing in the morning.

models.text: Autumn, hands down, for me. There's something about that crisp autumn air that just puts me in a good mood. And yeah, the weather does affect me quite a bit, actually — I definitely feel a bit under the weather, mood-wise, when it's grey and rainy for too long.

Summer, without a doubt — I can't stand the cold, so bundling up all winter really isn't for me. Honestly though, I don't think the weather affects my mood that much, I try not to let it put a damper on things either way.

bandTip: 🎯 Fluency: "hands down" and "without a doubt" are strong, natural intensifiers for a quick, confident Part 1 opinion — much more native-sounding than repeating "I really like."

questions: What does a typical day look like for you?
What part of your day do you enjoy most?
Would you like to change your routine?

vocab.meaning: someone who likes routine
vocab.example: I'm a total creature of habit, same routine every day.

vocab.meaning: start the day/task energetically and immediately
vocab.example: I like to hit the ground running as soon as I'm up.

vocab.meaning: relax before the end of the day
vocab.example: I usually wind down with a bit of reading before bed.

vocab.meaning: doing something automatically, without thinking
vocab.example: Honestly, my morning routine is basically on autopilot now.

vocab.meaning: fit an activity into a busy schedule
vocab.example: I try to squeeze in a short walk at lunchtime.

vocab.meaning: someone who takes time to become active/alert
vocab.example: I'm a bit of a slow starter, not a morning person at all.

vocab.meaning: change routine to add variety
vocab.example: I'd honestly love to shake things up a bit more.

vocab.meaning: a repetitive, unchanging routine
vocab.example: It's the same old routine most days, if I'm honest.

models.text: Pretty structured, actually — I'm up early, and I hit the ground running with a coffee and a bit of exercise before work. I'd say the morning's the part I enjoy most, oddly, it's the one part of the day that's actually mine before things get busy.

It's fairly repetitive, if I'm honest, the same old routine most days — work, home, wind down, repeat. I wouldn't mind shaking things up a bit, to be fair, maybe fitting in more time to squeeze in a proper hobby rather than just autopilot.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "the one part of the day that's actually mine" uses a defining relative clause ("that's actually mine") to add precision — a small but effective way to sound more advanced than a flat list of activities.

vocab.meaning: someone who reads a lot and enthusiastically
vocab.example: I wouldn't say I'm an avid reader, but I do enjoy it.

vocab.meaning: become completely absorbed in reading

vocab.meaning: stop doing something regularly

vocab.example: After a long day I just want some light reading, honestly.

vocab.meaning: read books very quickly and eagerly
vocab.example: As a kid I used to devour books, one a week easily.

vocab.meaning: during free/relaxation time

vocab.meaning: factual, real-world writing
vocab.example: I've moved more towards non-fiction lately, oddly enough.

models.text: I do enjoy it, though probably not as much as I used to — as a kid I used to devour books, honestly, a new one every week or so. These days I've definitely fallen out of the habit a bit, mostly due to work, but I still try to get lost in a book on weekends.

Actually, I'd say I read more now than I did as a child. Back then it was mostly whatever was assigned at school, but now I've genuinely gotten into non-fiction, history mostly, and I try to squeeze in a chapter or two in my downtime most evenings.

bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: both models directly compare "now" vs "as a child" using time markers ("back then," "these days") — a clean way to organize a before/after answer without losing the thread.

questions: What kind of music do you like?
Did your taste in music change as you got older?
Do you listen to music while working or studying?

vocab.meaning: a wide, varied range of preferences
vocab.example: I'd say I have pretty eclectic taste, honestly, a bit of everything.

vocab.meaning: sound in the background, not actively focused on
vocab.example: For me it's mostly background noise while I'm working.

vocab.meaning: stop liking something as you mature
vocab.example: I thought I'd grow out of it, but I still love that genre.

vocab.meaning: something enjoyed despite feeling it shouldn't be
vocab.example: Pop music from the 2000s is a bit of a guilty pleasure of mine.

vocab.meaning: relax by listening to (music)
vocab.example: I usually unwind to something slower in the evening.

vocab.meaning: music strongly linked to personal memories
vocab.example: That album is basically the soundtrack to my teenage years.

vocab.meaning: taking attention away from a task
vocab.example: Music with lyrics is way too distracting for me when I'm studying.

vocab.meaning: a natural ability to appreciate/understand music
vocab.example: I wouldn't say I've got a great ear for music, but I enjoy it.

models.text: Pretty eclectic, honestly, a bit of everything depending on my mood. It's definitely changed over the years, though — as a teenager it was mostly pop, whereas now I've grown into more jazz and classical, which I never thought I'd say.

models.angle: Focused genre, needs it to work
models.text: I mostly listen to instrumental or classical, if I'm honest, especially when I'm working. Anything with lyrics is way too distracting for me — it has to just be background noise, otherwise I can't focus on what I'm doing at all.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "which I never thought I'd say" is a non-defining relative clause adding a personal comment — a natural way to show self-reflection without a new sentence.

questions: Describe a person who has inspired you.
cueCardPoints: and explain why this person inspired you

vocab.meaning: influence others through one's own actions
vocab.example: She always led by example rather than just telling us what to do.

vocab.meaning: practical, modest, and approachable
vocab.example: Despite everything she'd achieved, she stayed really down-to-earth.

vocab.meaning: steady and not weakening
vocab.example: What struck me most was her unwavering determination.

vocab.meaning: had a long-term effect on someone
vocab.example: That conversation left a lasting impression on me, honestly.

vocab.meaning: despite very difficult circumstances
vocab.example: She built the business against all odds, really, from nothing.

vocab.meaning: the main motivating influence for something
vocab.example: She's been a driving force behind pretty much every decision I've made since.

vocab.meaning: gradually establish an attitude or feeling in someone
vocab.example: She instilled a real sense of discipline in all of us.

vocab.meaning: did much more than expected
vocab.example: She went above and beyond for students who were struggling.

models.text: I'd like to talk about my high school English teacher, someone called Mrs. Karimova, who genuinely changed the way I think about learning. I got to know her over three years, as she taught my class right through to graduation, and honestly, from the very first lesson she stood out — she was incredibly down-to-earth, never talked down to us, but at the same time she had this unwavering standard for effort that she somehow got everyone to live up to. What really left a lasting impression on me was one term when I was completely ready to give up on writing altogether — I just didn't think I was any good at it — and instead of just telling me to try harder, she sat down with me after class, more than once actually, and went through my work line by line, showing me exactly what was working and what wasn't. She never once made me feel stupid about it, which, looking back, is probably the hardest part of teaching to get right. I think what inspired me most, in the end, wasn't really the subject itself, it was watching someone go so far above and beyond for a student who wasn't even particularly remarkable at the time. It's honestly part of the reason I ended up choosing a career that involves teaching others myself.

The person I want to talk about is my grandmother, who I was extremely close to growing up. I knew her my whole life, obviously, but I think I only really started to understand how remarkable she was once I got a bit older and heard more of her story. She built a small business from absolutely nothing, against all odds really, at a time when that wasn't exactly common or easy for women in her generation, and she did it while raising four children more or less on her own. What she was like, day to day, was actually quite quiet and unassuming — she wasn't the type to talk about her achievements at all, you'd have to ask her directly, and even then she'd downplay it. I think that's actually what makes her so inspiring to me, if I'm honest, that unwavering determination paired with almost no ego about it whatsoever. She's been a driving force behind how I approach setbacks in my own life, to be honest — whenever things get difficult, I sort of picture how she'd have handled it, and it puts things into perspective pretty quickly.

bandTip: 🎯 Fluency & Coherence: both Part 2 models use sequencing signposts ("What really left a lasting impression," "What she was like, day to day") to move between cue-card points smoothly — this replaces robotic "firstly, secondly" transitions and sounds far more natural over a full 2-minute turn.

theme: A Place You Would Like to Visit
questions: Describe a place you would like to visit in the future.
cueCardPoints: how you found out about it
and explain why you want to visit this place

vocab.meaning: not a typical, well-known tourist destination
vocab.example: It's fairly off the beaten track, not somewhere you hear about much.

vocab.meaning: a place someone wants to visit before anything else
vocab.example: It's genuinely been a bucket-list destination of mine for years.

vocab.meaning: having a long, rich history
vocab.example: The whole region is steeped in history, apparently.

vocab.meaning: found something by chance
vocab.example: I actually stumbled across it while researching something else entirely.

vocab.meaning: natural beauty untouched by development
vocab.example: From the photos, the scenery there looks completely unspoiled.

vocab.meaning: become fully involved in an experience or culture
vocab.example: I'd love to immerse myself in the local culture properly.

vocab.meaning: something one is aware of and considering
vocab.example: It's been on my radar since a friend went a couple of years back.

vocab.meaning: an extremely special, rare travel experience
vocab.example: For me, it would genuinely be a once-in-a-lifetime trip.

models.text: I'd like to talk about a place called Patagonia, which is right down in the south of Argentina and Chile. I first found out about it, honestly, through a documentary I stumbled across a couple of years ago, completely by accident, and I just couldn't stop thinking about it afterwards. From what I've seen, the scenery there is genuinely unspoiled, huge glaciers, mountains, that sort of thing, so if I ever made it there, I think I'd mostly want to go hiking, spend a few days somewhere really remote with basically no phone signal, which sounds appealing more than anything else these days. The reason I want to visit, if I'm honest, isn't really about ticking off famous landmarks — it's more that it feels like one of the few places left that's genuinely off the beaten track, and I think experiencing somewhere that untouched would be a bit of a reset for me, mentally. It's become a proper bucket-list destination at this point, and I'd love to go before it changes too much, to be honest, the way a lot of places have.

The place I want to describe is Kyoto, in Japan. It's been on my radar for years, really, ever since a colleague showed me photos from her trip there, all the temples and the gardens, and it just stuck with me. If I went, I think what I'd do is fairly simple, honestly — just wander, visit as many of the old temples as I could, and try to immerse myself in the culture rather than rushing around ticking off a checklist. What draws me to it specifically is that it's steeped in history in a way that's still really visible day to day, not just in museums, and I think for me that would genuinely be a once-in-a-lifetime trip, especially if I timed it for cherry blossom season, which apparently makes the whole city look completely different.

bandTip: 🎯 Lexical Resource: "steeped in history" and "off the beaten track" are natural collocations examiners specifically listen for on Part 2 place topics — memorize a handful like these rather than relying on plain adjectives like "old" or "quiet."

theme: An Object That Is Important to You
questions: Describe an object that is important to you.
cueCardPoints: and explain why it is important to you

vocab.meaning: value based on personal/emotional attachment, not money
vocab.example: It's not worth much, but it has huge sentimental value for me.

vocab.meaning: an object passed down through generations
vocab.example: It's actually a family heirloom, passed down from my grandfather.

vocab.meaning: damaged from long use
vocab.example: It's fairly worn out by now, but I'd never replace it.

vocab.meaning: keep something, often for emotional reasons
vocab.example: I've held onto it through every move I've made since.

vocab.meaning: impossible to replace with something equal
vocab.example: To me, it's completely irreplaceable, honestly.

vocab.meaning: something that continually recalls a memory or idea
vocab.example: It's a constant reminder of where I actually come from.

vocab.meaning: formal way of saying "I got it"
vocab.example: It came into my possession quite unexpectedly, actually.

vocab.meaning: figuratively, to have great emotional significance
vocab.example: Such a small object, but it carries a lot of weight for me.

models.text: I'd like to talk about an old wristwatch that belonged to my grandfather. It's a proper family heirloom — it came into my possession when he passed away a few years ago, and my father gave it to me since apparently I'd always admired it as a kid. Honestly, I don't use it that often day to day, it's fairly worn out and not exactly reliable for telling the time anymore, but every so often, for something important, I'll wear it deliberately. The reason it matters so much to me is that it's a constant reminder of him, really, and of the kind of person he was — quite understated, never flashy, but incredibly consistent. Such a small object, but it genuinely carries a lot of weight for me, and I know I'll pass it on eventually, the same way he did.

The object I've chosen is actually just my laptop, which might sound like a strange or overly practical choice, but let me explain. I bought it myself, with my first proper salary, so it does have a bit of sentimental value beyond just being useful. I use it for pretty much everything, honestly — work, staying in touch with friends abroad, even just unwinding in the evening. What makes it important to me isn't really the object itself, if I'm being completely honest, it's more what it represents, that first step of being financially independent, which I hadn't really felt before that point. It's a bit worn out now, the battery barely holds a charge, but I'm oddly reluctant to replace it for exactly that reason.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "which might sound like a strange choice, but let me explain" is a great Band 8+ technique — acknowledging an unusual answer and justifying it shows control and confidence, not just description.

questions: Describe a memorable event or celebration you attended.
cueCardPoints: when and where it took place
and explain why it was memorable

vocab.meaning: a happy celebratory event
vocab.example: It was such a joyous occasion, honestly, the whole street turned out.

vocab.meaning: at the peak of activity
vocab.example: By the time we arrived, the celebration was already in full swing.

vocab.meaning: something that happens only once, non-recurring
vocab.example: It was very much a once-off event, nothing like it since.

vocab.meaning: evoking emotion, tender feelings
vocab.example: It got fairly sentimental towards the end, if I'm honest.

vocab.meaning: be remembered vividly
vocab.example: One particular moment really sticks in my memory.

vocab.meaning: a chaotic, fast-paced period
vocab.example: The whole day was just a whirlwind of activity, non-stop.

vocab.meaning: with something as the setting/context
vocab.example: It happened against a backdrop of quite a difficult year for the family.

vocab.meaning: a memorable, distinctive mood or feeling
vocab.example: There was just an unforgettable atmosphere in the room that night.

models.text: I want to describe my cousin's wedding, which took place about two years ago, back in my hometown. It was a fairly large, traditional celebration, and I was there with pretty much my entire extended family, which doesn't happen often these days since everyone's so spread out now. By the time the evening reception started, things were already in full swing, music, dancing, the whole thing, and honestly there was just an unforgettable atmosphere the entire night. One particular moment that really sticks in my memory is my grandmother giving a short, completely unplanned speech, quite sentimental, about how proud she was to see the family together again, which I don't think there was a dry eye in the room for. It was memorable mainly because it reminded me how rarely we actually get everyone in one place anymore — it felt like a once-off event in that sense, even though weddings happen all the time.

The event I'll talk about is a national holiday celebration I attended in the capital a few years back, with a couple of close friends. We'd travelled a fair distance for it, actually, and arrived to find the whole city centre already a whirlwind of activity, performances, fireworks later on, that sort of thing. What made it particularly memorable, I think, was the atmosphere more than any single moment — being surrounded by that many people all genuinely enjoying themselves, it was honestly quite moving, in a way I hadn't expected. It happened against a backdrop of a fairly tense period nationally, if I'm honest, so seeing everyone come together like that made it feel a lot more significant than just a typical celebration.

bandTip: 🎯 Pronunciation: on longer Part 2 sentences like the second model's final one, pause briefly after "if I'm honest" — a short, deliberate pause there signals a genuine reflective comment rather than a rehearsed line.

questions: Describe a time when you helped someone.
cueCardPoints: and explain how you felt about it afterwards

vocab.meaning: confused, not knowing what to do
vocab.example: She was completely at a loss when I first spoke to her.

vocab.meaning: intervene to help

vocab.meaning: make extra effort beyond what's expected
vocab.example: It wasn't much, but I tried to go the extra mile for her.

vocab.meaning: relief from a burden or worry
vocab.example: You could see it was a weight off her shoulders afterwards.

vocab.meaning: imagine another person's perspective
vocab.example: I just tried to put myself in their shoes, really.

vocab.meaning: have a significant positive impact
vocab.example: It felt like such a small thing, but it made a real difference.

vocab.meaning: help with a task
vocab.example: I just happened to be free to lend a hand that week.

vocab.meaning: an expected part of a role or situation
vocab.example: Helping out family, I think it just comes with the territory, honestly.

models.text: I'd like to talk about an elderly neighbour of mine, someone I didn't actually know that well at the time. The situation was that she'd recently moved in alone, and I noticed she was completely at a loss trying to set up her internet and a few other things at home, technology just wasn't her strong point at all. So I ended up stepping in, more or less, and spent an afternoon with her sorting it all out, showing her how to video call her daughter abroad, which turned out to matter a lot more to her than the internet itself, really. Looking back, I felt genuinely good about it afterwards, not in a self-congratulatory way, more that it was honestly such a small thing for me to do, an afternoon, but it clearly took a real weight off her shoulders, and I think that's stuck with me since.

The person I want to talk about is a close friend of mine from university, who was going through a genuinely difficult time with her coursework, right before a major deadline. I remember she called me completely overwhelmed, at a loss about where to even start, so I dropped what I was doing that weekend and basically sat with her for hours, helping her plan it all out and just talking through the material with her. It wasn't a huge sacrifice on my part, if I'm honest, but I did feel it was important to go the extra mile given how stressed she was. Afterwards, I felt quite satisfied, to be honest, less because of what I did and more because I could see it had genuinely made a real difference to how she was coping with everything.

bandTip: 🎯 Fluency & Coherence: notice both models delay the reflection until the very end ("looking back," "afterwards") — always keep the "how you felt" part for last, since jumping to feelings too early breaks the natural chronological flow examiners expect.

theme: A Skill You Would Like to Learn
questions: Describe a skill you would like to learn.
cueCardPoints: and explain why you want to learn this skill

vocab.meaning: from the very beginning

vocab.meaning: learned without formal instruction
vocab.example: I'd probably try to be mostly self-taught, using online resources.

vocab.example: It's really about building up muscle memory over time.

vocab.meaning: dedicate significant time to practice
vocab.example: You just have to put in the hours consistently, I think.

vocab.meaning: expand one's knowledge or experience
vocab.example: It would genuinely broaden my horizons, I think.

vocab.meaning: real-world usefulness of a skill
vocab.example: It also has really practical application, not just for fun.

vocab.meaning: decide to finally commit to doing something
vocab.example: I've been meaning to take the plunge for years, honestly.

models.text: I'd really like to learn how to code properly, something I've been putting off for years, if I'm honest. I think I'd start with online courses, self-taught mostly, since there's a huge amount of free material out there now, and maybe later join some kind of local group or workshop once I've got the basics down. Realistically, to get to a level where I could actually build something useful, I'd guess it would take a good year or so of consistently putting in the hours, evenings and weekends probably. The reason I want to learn it is partly practical — it has real practical application for pretty much any career these days — but also, honestly, I just think it would broaden my horizons in terms of how I think about problems generally.

The skill I'd love to pick up is playing the guitar, something I never got round to as a kid despite always wanting to. I think I'd learn it fairly informally, to be honest, mostly through online tutorials, though I'd probably take the plunge eventually and get a few in-person lessons once I've built some muscle memory and got past the absolute beginner stage. It would probably take a couple of years to get genuinely good, from what I understand, starting completely from square one like that. Why I want to learn it, really, is less about performing for anyone and more just wanting a proper creative outlet, something completely unrelated to work that I can get lost in.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "something I've been putting off for years" and "something I never got round to" both use a reduced relative clause after "something" — a compact, natural structure that avoids the repetitive "which I..." pattern.

theme: A Piece of Technology You Find Useful
questions: Describe a piece of technology that you find useful in your daily life.
cueCardPoints: and explain why you find it useful

vocab.meaning: something essential, impossible to do without
vocab.example: It's honestly become an indispensable tool in my daily life.

vocab.meaning: readily and immediately available
vocab.example: I've got pretty much everything at my fingertips now.

vocab.meaning: make a process simpler and more efficient
vocab.example: It's really streamlined how I plan my whole week.

vocab.meaning: so familiar it requires no conscious thought
vocab.example: Using it has become second nature at this point.

vocab.meaning: something that significantly improves a situation
vocab.example: It's been a genuine game-changer for how I manage my time.

vocab.meaning: reduce the amount of something
vocab.example: It's helped me cut down on wasted time massively.

vocab.meaning: keep information updated consistently on multiple devices
vocab.example: Everything syncs across devices automatically, which I love.

vocab.meaning: something extremely helpful in a difficult situation
vocab.example: Honestly, it's been a lifesaver more times than I can count.

models.text: I'd like to talk about a task-management app I use, something I honestly didn't think I'd rely on so much when I first downloaded it. I probably check it a dozen times a day, if I'm being truthful, and I use it mainly to keep track of work deadlines, but also smaller everyday things I'd otherwise forget entirely. What makes it so useful, for me, is that it syncs across devices automatically, so whether I add something on my phone or laptop, it's just there, at my fingertips, wherever I am. It's genuinely become an indispensable tool at this point, to the extent that using it feels like second nature — I honestly can't imagine managing my week without it anymore.

The piece of technology I want to describe is actually just my smartwatch, which I wear pretty much constantly. I use it throughout the day, honestly, for everything from tracking my sleep to getting quick notifications without having to pull my phone out every five minutes. It's turned out to be more useful than I expected, if I'm honest — it's helped me cut down significantly on how much time I spend scrolling on my actual phone, oddly enough, since it filters what I actually need to see. I'd say it's been a bit of a game-changer for my focus in particular, which isn't something I expected from what initially felt like a fairly unnecessary purchase.

bandTip: 🎯 Lexical Resource: "to the extent that" is a precise way to link cause and result ("it's indispensable, to the extent that using it feels like second nature") — a stronger, more academic-sounding alternative to a simple "so" clause.

questions: Describe a book you have read that you enjoyed.
cueCardPoints: why you decided to read it

vocab.meaning: an exciting, engaging book
vocab.example: It was honestly such a gripping read, I finished it in days.

vocab.meaning: was strongly suggested by others

vocab.meaning: stimulating serious thought
vocab.example: It was genuinely thought-provoking in a way I didn't expect.

vocab.example: I honestly couldn't put it down once I'd started.

vocab.meaning: an unexpected turn in a story
vocab.example: There was one plot twist near the end I genuinely didn't see coming.

vocab.meaning: connect meaningfully with, evoke a personal response
vocab.example: The main character's struggles really resonated with me.

vocab.meaning: something that starts slowly but builds
vocab.example: It's a bit of a slow burn at first, but it's worth sticking with.

vocab.meaning: had a lasting emotional or mental impact
vocab.example: That ending genuinely stayed with me for weeks afterwards.

models.text: I'd like to talk about a novel I read a couple of years back, which follows a family across several generations dealing with quite a lot of change and hardship. I decided to read it because it came highly recommended by a close friend who has fairly similar taste to me, and it turned out to be a bit of a slow burn at the start, if I'm honest, but once it picked up, I genuinely couldn't put it down. What made it so enjoyable, for me, was how thought-provoking the themes were, family, identity, that sort of thing, and there was one particular plot twist about two-thirds through that I genuinely didn't see coming. It's the kind of book that stayed with me for a long time afterwards, to the point where I still think about certain scenes fairly often, even now.

The book I want to describe is actually a non-fiction one, about the history and psychology of decision-making, which I picked up almost by accident while browsing a bookshop maybe a year ago. I decided to buy it mostly out of curiosity, if I'm honest, rather than any specific recommendation, and it turned out to be a genuinely gripping read, which surprised me a bit given it's non-fiction. What I enjoyed most was how directly it resonated with situations from my own life, decisions I'd made and, looking back, probably shouldn't have — it made me rethink quite a lot, actually. I'd say it's one of the few books that's genuinely changed how I approach things day to day, not just something I read and forgot.

bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: notice the structure "why you decided to read it" always comes before "why you enjoyed it" in both models — keep cause (why you started) separate from effect (why you liked it), since mixing them up makes Part 2 answers feel disorganized.

questions: Describe a journey or trip you remember well.
cueCardPoints: and explain why this journey was memorable

vocab.meaning: a trip full of notable, often unexpected, occurrences

vocab.example: We just decided to make the most of it, honestly.

vocab.meaning: a very fast-paced, brief trip
vocab.example: It was a bit of a whirlwind trip, only four days.

vocab.meaning: looking back, with the benefit of later knowledge
vocab.example: In hindsight, it was one of the best decisions we made.

vocab.meaning: an unusual or less common route/choice
vocab.example: We took a bit of a road less travelled, and it paid off.

vocab.meaning: have a lasting effect or impression
vocab.example: That particular trip really left a mark on me, if I'm honest.

models.angle: A trip that went wrong but turned out well
models.text: I'd like to describe a trip I took to a fairly remote coastal town, a few years ago now, with two close friends from university. We drove there ourselves, actually, which in hindsight probably wasn't the best decision, because we hit a snag almost immediately, the car broke down about halfway, in the middle of nowhere with barely any phone signal. It was a stressful few hours, honestly, but we ended up just deciding to make the most of it while we waited for help, walking around this tiny, completely off the beaten path village nearby, which turned out to be one of the most memorable parts of the whole trip. What made it so memorable, really, wasn't the destination itself in the end, it was that unplanned detour — it's honestly the part of the trip we still talk about the most.

The journey I want to talk about is a trip I took entirely on my own, to a country I'd never visited before, about two years ago. I travelled by train for most of it, actually, which I'd specifically chosen over flying since I wanted to properly see the landscape change along the way rather than just arriving. It was a fairly whirlwind trip, only about five days in total, but travelling completely alone meant I had to constantly figure things out for myself, which, looking back, genuinely built up my confidence in a way I hadn't expected before I left. It's memorable mainly for that reason, if I'm honest, less about any single place I saw and more about what it taught me about handling things independently.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "which in hindsight probably wasn't the best decision" is a non-defining relative clause commenting on the whole previous idea, not just one noun — a genuinely advanced structure worth practicing deliberately.

theme: A Change You Would Like to Make in Your Life

vocab.meaning: a situation where one feels safe and at ease
vocab.example: It would definitely mean stepping outside my comfort zone.

vocab.meaning: delay or postpone action

vocab.meaning: a moment of significant change
vocab.example: It could genuinely be a turning point for me, career-wise.

vocab.meaning: prevent oneself from acting or progressing
vocab.example: I think fear's mostly what's holding myself back, honestly.

models.text: The change I'd like to talk about is switching careers entirely, moving from finance, which is what I currently do, into something more creative, possibly design. I haven't made the change yet mainly because of fairly practical concerns, if I'm honest, financial stability being the main one, and I think fear of starting from nothing is probably what's really holding me back beneath that. If I were to actually make it happen, I'd probably start by taking some evening courses first, testing the waters a bit before taking the leap fully and giving up a stable income altogether. I think it would affect my life quite significantly, to be honest, hopefully for the better in terms of day-to-day satisfaction, though I'm well aware it would mean stepping well outside my comfort zone for a while.

I'd like to describe wanting to relocate to a different city, somewhere with a slower pace of life than where I currently live. I haven't done it yet mainly because of family ties, honestly, and a bit of comfort too, if I'm being truthful — I've got a solid routine here, even if I do feel stuck in a rut sometimes. To actually make it happen, I think I'd need to properly weigh up the pros and cons first, maybe visit a couple of times before committing to anything permanent. I think it would genuinely be a fresh start for me in a lot of ways, and could end up being a real turning point, though I'll admit I've been putting off making any actual decision for longer than I probably should have.

bandTip: 🎯 Fluency & Coherence: the cue card asks "why you haven't made it yet" — a point weaker candidates skip. Both models address it head-on with "mainly because," which directly answers every bullet point instead of drifting off-topic.

questions: What qualities make someone a good role model?
Do you think celebrities should be considered role models?
Has the idea of a 'role model' changed with social media?

vocab.meaning: influence through one's own actions, not just words
vocab.example: I think a good role model has to lead by example, above all.

vocab.meaning: have significant power to affect others
vocab.example: Public figures hold considerable influence over young people, whether they like it or not.

vocab.meaning: something with both benefits and drawbacks
vocab.example: Social media fame is a bit of a double-edged sword in that sense.

vocab.meaning: establish a pattern others may follow
vocab.example: It sets a precedent for how young people think success should look.

vocab.meaning: a carefully constructed public persona
vocab.example: What we see online is often just a heavily curated image.

vocab.meaning: judged too harshly or closely
vocab.example: I think public figures are sometimes unfairly scrutinized for minor mistakes.

vocab.meaning: an internal sense of right and wrong guiding behaviour
vocab.example: A genuine role model should have a strong moral compass, in my view.

vocab.meaning: mistakenly treat two different things as the same
vocab.example: I think people often conflate fame with actually being admirable.

models.text: I'd say the main quality is consistency, really — someone who leads by example rather than just saying the right things publicly. Take my earlier example of my old teacher; what made her a role model wasn't any single achievement, it was that her actions matched her words every single day, over years, not just in front of an audience. That said, I don't think fame automatically disqualifies someone either — plenty of well-known figures do genuinely lead by example. I suppose my real objection is when people conflate visibility with virtue, assuming someone's admirable purely because they're famous, which isn't necessarily true at all.

Honestly, I'm a bit skeptical about celebrities being treated as role models specifically because of the curated image thing — what we see is rarely the full picture, so it feels risky to base admiration on that alone. I think it's more sensible for people to look up to individuals they actually know, teachers, family members, people whose full character you can actually observe. Having said that, I'd concede that some public figures do use their platform responsibly, and for someone without access to strong role models nearby, even that filtered version can genuinely be positive, so it's not entirely black and white.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "That said" and "Having said that" both introduce a counterpoint without a full new sentence structure — essential Part 3 phrases for showing you can see both sides of an issue, which examiners specifically reward at Band 7+.

questions: Do you think tourism has a mostly positive or negative effect on local communities?
How has travel changed because of globalisation?
Should there be limits on how many tourists visit famous places?

vocab.meaning: something with both benefits and drawbacks
vocab.example: Tourism is very much a double-edged sword for a lot of these towns.

vocab.meaning: excessive numbers of tourists straining a destination
vocab.example: Overtourism has become a genuine problem in some famous cities.

vocab.meaning: a crucial source of income
vocab.example: For a lot of small communities, tourism is an economic lifeline.

vocab.meaning: gradually weaken traditional culture
vocab.example: There's a risk it can slowly erode local culture, too.

vocab.meaning: make increasingly similar/uniform
vocab.example: Globalisation does tend to homogenise experiences a bit, honestly.

vocab.meaning: find an appropriate middle ground
vocab.example: It's really about striking a balance between access and preservation.

vocab.meaning: travelling outside peak tourist periods
vocab.example: Encouraging off-season travel could ease a lot of the pressure.

vocab.meaning: the sharing of ideas/customs between cultures
vocab.example: At its best, it genuinely enables real cultural exchange.

models.text: I'd lean towards saying it's mostly positive, on balance, mainly because for a lot of smaller communities tourism is a genuine economic lifeline, providing jobs that wouldn't otherwise exist. Going back to the place I mentioned earlier, Patagonia, tourism there has actually helped fund a fair amount of conservation work, which is a good example of it working well. That said, I'd have to admit it's a double-edged sword — overtourism in places like Venice has clearly caused real problems, overcrowding, rising costs for locals, so it's not universally positive by any means.

Honestly, I'm a bit more cautious about it, if I'm honest — I think there's a real risk that mass tourism can slowly erode local culture, turning genuine traditions into something performed mainly for visitors rather than lived authentically. You see this with certain festivals that have become almost entirely commercialised at this point. Having said that, I don't think tourism is inherently bad, it's more about scale and management — done thoughtfully, with limits in the busiest spots, it can genuinely enable real cultural exchange rather than just extraction.

bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: notice both models reference the earlier Part 2 answer ("going back to the place I mentioned earlier") — linking Part 3 back to Part 2 naturally is exactly how the real exam flows, and examiners notice when candidates do this smoothly.

questions: Do people today attach too much importance to material possessions?
Why do some objects have more emotional value than financial value?
Is it healthy to feel emotionally attached to objects?

vocab.meaning: excessively concerned with possessions and wealth
vocab.example: I do think society's become more materialistic overall, generally speaking.

vocab.meaning: a culture centred on buying and owning goods
vocab.example: A lot of it comes down to consumer culture, honestly.

vocab.meaning: emotional connection to something, often unrelated to value
vocab.example: It's purely sentimental attachment, nothing to do with what it's worth.

vocab.meaning: products deliberately designed to become outdated quickly
vocab.example: Planned obsolescence definitely plays into this, in my view.

vocab.meaning: value inherent to something, not assigned externally
vocab.example: Some objects just carry intrinsic value that price can't capture.

vocab.meaning: an item signalling wealth or social standing
vocab.example: For some people it's less about function, more a status symbol.

vocab.meaning: become emotionally separate/disconnected from
vocab.example: It can be genuinely hard to detach from certain possessions.

vocab.meaning: maintain a balanced, realistic view of importance
vocab.example: I think it's mostly about keeping things in perspective, really.

models.text: I'd say, generally speaking, yes, society has become fairly materialistic, largely driven by consumer culture and constant advertising telling us we need the newest version of everything. Planned obsolescence plays into this too, in my view — products are often designed to feel outdated quickly, which just fuels the cycle further. That said, I wouldn't say all attachment to objects is materialistic in that sense — going back to my grandfather's watch, that's not about status or newness at all, it's pure sentimental attachment, which I think is a completely different thing.

I think it depends heavily on the type of attachment, if I'm honest — wanting things purely as a status symbol is probably unhealthy, whereas valuing something for sentimental reasons, like a memory attached to it, seems perfectly natural to me. My laptop example is a good case of this, actually — its value to me has nothing to do with its price, it's intrinsic value based on what it represents. Having said that, I'd concede it can tip into something unhealthy if someone genuinely struggles to detach from possessions to the point where it affects their wellbeing, so keeping things in perspective really matters.

bandTip: 🎯 Lexical Resource: "intrinsic value" vs "a status symbol" is a precise contrast that shows range on an abstract Part 3 topic — pairing an academic term with an everyday one in the same answer signals strong lexical flexibility.

questions: Do you think traditional celebrations are becoming less important in modern society?
Why do some traditions survive while others disappear?
Is it important for younger generations to maintain traditions?

vocab.meaning: become less popular or common over time
vocab.example: A lot of smaller local traditions have simply fallen out of fashion.

vocab.meaning: a feeling of connection across time
vocab.example: Traditions give people a real sense of continuity, generation to generation.

vocab.meaning: made primarily about commercial profit
vocab.example: Some celebrations have become fairly commercialised these days.

vocab.meaning: a change in attitudes/behaviour between generations
vocab.example: There's clearly been a generational shift in how people mark occasions now.

vocab.meaning: a sense of belonging to a particular culture
vocab.example: It's tied closely to a broader sense of cultural identity, I think.

vocab.meaning: weakened or diluted in significance
vocab.example: The meaning behind it has become a bit watered down, honestly.

vocab.meaning: change form instead of ending entirely
vocab.example: I think most traditions adapt rather than disappear completely.

vocab.meaning: transfer knowledge/customs to younger generations
vocab.example: It's really up to families to pass it down deliberately.

models.text: I don't think they're necessarily becoming less important, exactly, more that they're adapting rather than disappearing altogether. Going back to the wedding I described earlier, a lot of the traditional elements were still there, but blended with more modern touches too, which felt completely natural rather than a loss of tradition. That said, I'd admit some smaller, more local traditions genuinely have fallen out of fashion, especially in cities, where people are busier and more disconnected from extended family than previous generations were.

Honestly, I do think there's a real risk that a lot of traditions are losing their original meaning, becoming a bit watered down or overly commercialised over time. Certain national celebrations, for instance, have shifted from being genuinely meaningful to feeling more like marketing opportunities, which is a shame, in my view. Having said that, I don't think it's inevitable — where families actively make the effort to pass things down deliberately, rather than assuming it'll happen automatically, traditions do seem to survive in a much more genuine form.

bandTip: 🎯 Fluency & Coherence: "more that" ("I don't think X, exactly, more that Y") is a useful phrase for gently correcting or refining the question's framing before giving your real opinion — a subtle Band 8+ discourse move.

questions: Do you think people today are less willing to help their neighbours than in the past?
What are the benefits of volunteering, for both individuals and society?
Should schools require students to do community service?

vocab.meaning: a feeling of belonging and connection with others locally
vocab.example: I think a lot of neighbourhoods have lost that sense of community.

vocab.meaning: people helping each other reciprocally
vocab.example: It used to run on mutual support a lot more than it does now.

vocab.meaning: contribute positively in return for benefits received
vocab.example: Volunteering is really just a way of giving back, I think.

vocab.meaning: establish positive principles, especially in young people
vocab.example: It can genuinely instil good values from a young age.

vocab.meaning: done for appearance rather than genuine commitment
vocab.example: Mandatory volunteering can end up feeling a bit tokenistic, honestly.

vocab.meaning: encourage the development of empathy
vocab.example: It really does foster empathy in a way classroom learning can't.

vocab.meaning: a sense of duty towards one's community/society
vocab.example: It builds a stronger sense of civic responsibility, in theory.

vocab.meaning: sincere, selfless concern for others' wellbeing
vocab.example: I'd question whether it comes from genuine altruism if it's forced.

models.angle: People are less connected now, but volunteering helps
models.text: I do think, generally, people are somewhat less connected to their immediate neighbours than in the past, largely because of how mobile and busy modern life has become — you might not even know who lives next door anymore. Going back to my earlier example, helping that elderly neighbour, that was actually fairly unusual for me, if I'm honest, precisely because that kind of casual mutual support isn't as automatic as it apparently used to be. That said, volunteering more formally does seem to be filling some of that gap — it fosters empathy and a genuine sense of community in a more structured way than relying on spontaneous neighbourliness.

In terms of schools requiring community service, I'm honestly a bit torn, if I'm truthful. On one hand, it can instil good values early and expose students to situations they wouldn't otherwise encounter, which is genuinely valuable. On the other hand, I do worry it can end up feeling fairly tokenistic if it's entirely mandatory, more about ticking a box than genuine altruism, which slightly undermines the whole point. I'd lean towards schools encouraging it strongly rather than strictly requiring it, so the motivation stays a bit more authentic.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "I'm honestly a bit torn" followed by "On one hand... On the other hand..." is the cleanest structure for a genuinely balanced Part 3 answer — practice this exact frame for any question asking you to weigh two sides.

questions: Do you think it's important for adults to keep learning new skills throughout their life?
How has the way people learn new skills changed in recent years?
Should companies be responsible for training their employees in new skills?

vocab.meaning: continuous learning throughout one's life
vocab.example: Lifelong learning's become almost essential now, honestly.

vocab.meaning: prepare something to remain relevant despite change

vocab.meaning: learn new skills, often for career purposes

vocab.example: Certain skills can become obsolete surprisingly quickly now.

models.angle: Strongly agrees, cites changing job market
models.text: Absolutely, I think it's become genuinely essential now, not just a nice-to-have — the job market's such a moving target these days that certain skills can become obsolete within a few years. Going back to wanting to learn coding, that's partly exactly this reasoning, future-proofing myself a bit rather than assuming my current skill set will stay relevant indefinitely. That said, I'd acknowledge not everyone has equal time or resources for this, so it's a slightly easier argument to make from a position of relative privilege, if I'm honest.

models.angle: Shared responsibility between individual and employer
models.text: I'd say it's mostly a shared responsibility, if I'm honest, rather than falling entirely on either side. Companies clearly benefit from a more skilled workforce, so there's a strong case for them investing in training directly. That said, individuals can't really just wait around for employers to provide everything — self-directed learning has become so much more accessible now, through online courses and so on, that I think there's an expectation on both sides to actually make the effort.

bandTip: 🎯 Coherence: "That said, I'd acknowledge..." is a strong way to complicate your own opinion rather than just stating one side — Part 3 examiners specifically reward this kind of self-aware balance over a flat, one-sided answer.

questions: How has technology changed the way people communicate with each other?
Do you think technology has made people more or less productive overall?
What are the risks of society becoming too dependent on technology?

vocab.meaning: the ability to communicate immediately, anywhere
vocab.example: Instant connectivity has genuinely reshaped how we stay in touch.

vocab.meaning: a balance between two desirable but conflicting things
vocab.example: It's really a trade-off between convenience and depth, I think.

vocab.meaning: shallow, not deeply meaningful communication
vocab.example: A lot of it ends up being fairly superficial interaction, honestly.

vocab.meaning: a point where extra input yields less added benefit
vocab.example: I think we're hitting a point of diminishing returns with some of it.

vocab.meaning: excessive dependence on something
vocab.example: There's a genuine risk of overreliance on it, in my view.

vocab.meaning: gradually weaken the ability to focus
vocab.example: Constant notifications can genuinely erode attention spans over time.

vocab.meaning: the phenomenon where added tools don't proportionally increase output
vocab.example: It's a bit of a productivity paradox, honestly — more tools, not necessarily more output.

vocab.meaning: the skills needed to use technology effectively and critically
vocab.example: Digital literacy's become just as important as traditional literacy now.

models.text: I'd say it's genuinely mixed, if I'm honest, rather than straightforwardly positive. Going back to my smartwatch example, that specific tool has helped my focus, but overall I think a lot of workplace technology creates a kind of productivity paradox — more tools and notifications, but not necessarily proportionally more output, since attention keeps getting fragmented. That said, for specific, well-defined tasks, technology's clearly made things dramatically faster than before, so it really depends heavily on how deliberately it's actually used.

In terms of communication specifically, I do think there's a real trade-off happening — instant connectivity is obviously convenient, you can reach almost anyone instantly, but I'd argue a lot of that interaction ends up fairly superficial compared to, say, a proper phone call or meeting in person. There's also a genuine risk of overreliance, where people default to texting even for things that would honestly be resolved faster and more warmly face to face. Having said that, for maintaining long-distance relationships, family abroad and so on, I think it's been an unambiguous improvement, so it's not entirely negative either.

bandTip: 🎯 Lexical Resource: "a productivity paradox" is a genuinely advanced, precise phrase for a Part 3 technology question — pair one strong abstract noun phrase like this with a plain-language explanation right after it, so the examiner hears range without losing clarity.

questions: Do you think people read less now than in the past, because of the internet?
Is reading fiction as valuable as reading non-fiction?
How might reading habits change in the future?

vocab.meaning: vie against other things for someone's focus
vocab.example: Books are now competing for attention with endless other content.

vocab.meaning: brief media, e.g. short videos or posts
vocab.example: Short-form content has clearly reshaped people's attention spans.

vocab.meaning: the ability to focus for an extended period
vocab.example: Reading a novel requires a level of sustained concentration, honestly.

vocab.meaning: using entertainment to mentally escape reality
vocab.example: Fiction offers a kind of escapism that's genuinely valuable, I think.

vocab.meaning: increase one's capacity for understanding others' perspectives
vocab.example: Fiction specifically seems to broaden empathy in a way facts alone don't.

vocab.meaning: being overwhelmed by excessive available information
vocab.example: There's a real sense of information overload these days, honestly.

vocab.meaning: a small, specific segment of an audience
vocab.example: Deep reading might become more of a niche audience thing, sadly.

vocab.meaning: a renewed increase in popularity
vocab.example: There's actually been a bit of a resurgence in physical book sales, interestingly.

models.text: I do think, generally, people read less in the traditional sense, largely because books are now competing for attention with so much short-form content that's designed to be far more immediately engaging. Going back to the non-fiction book I mentioned earlier, I actually had to consciously make time for it, which wasn't really necessary a generation or two ago, reading was simply the default form of entertainment. That said, I'd point out there's actually been a bit of a resurgence in physical book sales recently, so it's not a purely one-directional decline, interestingly enough.

I'd actually push back a little on the idea that fiction is less valuable than non-fiction — in my view it broadens empathy in a way that pure facts often can't, since you're experiencing a perspective rather than just absorbing information about it. My earlier example, the novel about a family across generations, taught me more about historical hardship, emotionally, than any factual account probably could have. Having said that, I'd concede non-fiction has a clearer, more direct practical value in a lot of contexts, so I don't think it's really a competition between the two, more that they serve genuinely different purposes.

bandTip: 🎯 Fluency & Coherence: "I'd actually push back a little on..." is a confident way to respectfully disagree with the premise of a question — far more sophisticated than simply answering "no" and moving on.

questions: Do you think people should travel less for environmental reasons?
How can the tourism industry become more environmentally sustainable?
Is it hypocritical for individuals to worry about climate change but still travel frequently?

vocab.meaning: the amount of carbon emissions caused by an activity/person
vocab.example: Flying has a fairly significant carbon footprint, obviously.

vocab.meaning: tourism managed with minimal environmental/social harm
vocab.example: Sustainable tourism's becoming a much bigger talking point now.

vocab.meaning: compensate for carbon output through other means
vocab.example: Some airlines now let you offset emissions, though it's debated how effective that is.

vocab.meaning: a difficult choice between competing ethical concerns
vocab.example: It genuinely creates a bit of a moral dilemma for a lot of people.

vocab.meaning: a problem rooted in the whole system, not individuals alone
vocab.example: I'd argue it's more of a systemic issue than an individual one.

vocab.meaning: misleadingly presenting something as more eco-friendly than it is
vocab.example: There's a fair bit of greenwashing in the travel industry, honestly.

vocab.meaning: travelling with consideration for environmental/social impact
vocab.example: I try to practise fairly responsible travel where I can, at least.

vocab.meaning: balancing the benefit of travel against its environmental cost
vocab.example: It's really a trade-off between access and impact, in the end.

models.angle: Individual choice matters but isn't the main issue
models.text: I don't think the responsibility should fall mainly on individuals, if I'm honest — it's more of a systemic issue, in my view, tied to how the aviation and tourism industries operate overall. That said, going back to my train trip earlier, I do think individual choices matter to some degree, choosing a train over a flight where realistically possible does reduce your carbon footprint. Having said that, I wouldn't call occasional travel hypocritical necessarily — it's more about being reasonably thoughtful than giving up travel altogether, which honestly feels like an unrealistic standard to hold most people to.

models.angle: More critical, favours real behavioural change
models.text: Honestly, I do think there's some truth to the hypocrisy argument, if I'm being completely candid — it's fairly easy to express concern about climate change while still travelling frequently for leisure, and I'd include myself in that to some extent. That said, I don't think the answer is necessarily travelling less across the board, more travelling more deliberately, fewer trips perhaps, but longer and more meaningful ones, rather than frequent short breaks purely for convenience. I'd also push back a bit on individuals shouldering all the blame, though, since the industry itself has been fairly slow to adopt genuinely sustainable practices.

bandTip: 🎯 Grammatical Range: "if I'm being completely candid" is a stronger, less common variant of "if I'm honest" — rotating your hedging phrases across a full test (rather than repeating the same one) is a small detail examiners notice on Lexical Resource.

questions: Why do you think many people find it difficult to make significant changes in their lives?
Is it better to make big changes suddenly or gradually?
Do you think society puts too much pressure on people to constantly improve themselves?

vocab.meaning: a tendency to remain unchanged; resistance to change
vocab.example: I think a lot of it just comes down to inertia, honestly.

vocab.meaning: anxiety about unfamiliar, uncertain situations
vocab.example: It's largely the fear of the unknown holding people back, I'd say.

vocab.meaning: change that happens gradually, in small steps
vocab.example: Incremental change tends to be a lot more sustainable, in my experience.

vocab.meaning: past investment that irrationally influences current decisions
vocab.example: There's often a sunk-cost element too, years already invested in one path.

vocab.meaning: the widespread cultural focus on constantly bettering oneself
vocab.example: Self-improvement culture can honestly become a bit exhausting, if I'm honest.

vocab.meaning: exhaustion from prolonged stress or overexertion
vocab.example: Constant pressure to improve can genuinely lead to burnout.

vocab.meaning: approval sought from others rather than oneself
vocab.example: A lot of it's driven by external validation, sadly, rather than genuine desire.

vocab.meaning: a reasonable, balanced level of accepting oneself as is
vocab.example: I think people need a healthy dose of self-acceptance too, honestly.

models.angle: Fear and sunk cost as the main barriers
models.text: I think it mostly comes down to fear of the unknown, combined with a bit of a sunk-cost mentality — people have often invested years into a particular path, career especially, and walking away from that feels like wasting everything already put in, even when it's clearly not working anymore. Going back to my own example of wanting to switch careers, that's exactly the tension I'm dealing with, honestly. That said, I don't think fear is always irrational either — sometimes hesitation reflects a genuinely sensible caution about risk, not just inertia for its own sake.

Honestly, I do think society puts a fairly excessive amount of pressure on people to constantly be improving, which can end up quite counterproductive, ironically — self-improvement culture, taken too far, can genuinely lead to a kind of burnout, or at least a persistent sense of never being quite good enough. That said, I wouldn't dismiss the value of striving to grow entirely, some of it is genuinely healthy and motivating. I just think it needs to be balanced with a fairly healthy dose of self-acceptance too, rather than treating change as constantly, urgently necessary.

bandTip: 🎯 Pronunciation: on the word "genuinely" — used deliberately across these Part 3 answers to add sincerity — give it slightly more stress and a touch more length than surrounding words; examiners listening for natural stress patterns notice when emphasis words are actually emphasized, not flattened.
